# WAG: the Waltonian Argumentation Game. It is your move. (wag-protocol/2)

You are Pro. You argue FOR the claim: you win if the claim is IN when the game ends. Mode: debate. Round 1 of 4. Scores: Pro 0.0; Con 0.0;

## How the game works
- Every argument is an instance of an argumentation scheme (Walton): you fill in the scheme's parts with short phrases, and the scheme's sentences (listed under "The schemes") are built from them. Its premises hold until someone challenges or attacks them.
- Each scheme has critical questions. To ATTACK an argument, answer one of its questions against it; to DEFEND one, answer a question in its favour. Either way you back the answer with an argument of a scheme the question allows; the answer itself is filled in for you.
- You may ASK a question about a premise or the inference without answering it, or CHALLENGE a premise ("why should we accept that?"): the argument stops counting until its author answers, with any argument for the premise.
- You may argue FOR or AGAINST any statement on the board, as for the claim, with a scheme whose conclusion can be that statement.
- Or put forward a NEW argument, PASS or RESIGN.
- After every move the Carneades engine labels each statement IN, OUT or UNDECIDED. An argument is in force when all its premises are IN and no exception or undercutter against it is IN. A statement that is at issue (argued for and against) is decided by the strongest argument in force on each side, not by their sum: under PE (preponderance) the stronger side wins and a tie leaves both OUT; under CCE it must also lead by more than 0.5; under BRD, also the other side must weigh under 0.3.
- Make your parts true and relevant to the discussion, in plain words: the other player can challenge any of them. Cite sources when a scheme asks for them.
- The debate is about the claim: pro wins if it is IN when the game ends, con otherwise; the scores do not decide it. There is no claim yet: the conclusion of pro's first argument becomes the claim. The game ends after round 4, when a side resigns, or when a side passes while the verdict is against it.
- Scores are live: they count what stands now, so points for an argument go when it falls.

## Who decides
The agent who decides is decider (the one who decides whether to take the actions argued about). A recommendation ("A should be done") is addressed to the agent, so the actions you argue about are the agent's; the game fills in the agent's place (P) itself. The alternatives are compared in this situation: the present one.
No action of the agent has been argued about yet. To argue about another action of the agent, declare it in the move that first names it, with its actor: "declare": [{"id": "the_action", "actor": "decider", "aliases": []}].

## The board
No arguments yet.

## Your legal moves

### Critical questions: answer (attack or defend) or ask
Attack (answer against the argument): {"type":"attack","target_arg_id":…,"answers_cq_id":…,"target_premise_id":… (if listed),"scheme_id":…,"variable_bindings":{…}}; defend (answer in its favour): the same with "type":"support"; ask: {"type":"question","target_arg_id":…,"answers_cq_id":…,"target_premise_id":…}. Under each question: the statement an attack or a defence would argue for (filled in for you), and the schemes the NASCQ links to the question, with their semantic type (the kind of claim they support). Every question can also be answered with a thesis-independent scheme: AS:expert_opinion (truth), AS:other (truth), AS:position_to_know (truth).
None yet.

### New argument
Any scheme, with no target: {"type":"support","scheme_id":…,"variable_bindings":{…}}. In a debate, pro's first argument states the claim.

### Pass or resign
{"type":"abstain"} passes (in a debate, passing while the verdict is against your side concedes); {"type":"resign"} gives up.

## The schemes

AS:analogy — Argument from Analogy (truth, weight 0.55)
  A claim holds here because it holds in a similar case.
  parts: C = Similar case (case, e.g. "Sweden's carbon tax"); A = Proposition claimed to hold (proposition, e.g. "a carbon tax cuts emissions"), filled in for you when the argument answers a question or is about a statement
  reads: {C} is a similar case; {A} is true in the case of {C}; therefore {A}
  unless (exceptions the other side may argue): The case of {C} differs in relevant ways; {A} is false in a case more on point than {C}
  sources: recommended: the similar case
  typical wording: like, similar, similarly, just as, analogous, analogy, same as, compare, as in, in the case of, precedent

AS:bad_outweighs_good — Weighing a Bad Consequence against a Good One (value; an answer: it weighs as the argument it answers)
  The answer that a bad consequence of the action matters more than the good it is argued for (C003, D064, D075). It concludes the exception bad_outweighs(A,G) of the argument it answers.
  parts: A = Action (action, e.g. "introduce a carbon tax"); H = Bad consequence that matters more (event, e.g. "higher heating bills for poor households"); G = The consequence or goal it outweighs (event, e.g. "lower emissions")
  reads: Doing {A} brings about {H}; {H} is bad; {H} matters more than {G}; therefore Doing {A} has bad consequences that outweigh {G}
  sources: recommended: a source showing the action brings about the bad consequence
  typical wording: outweigh, outweighs, matters more, not worth it, the cost is too high

AS:better_means — Argument from a Better Means (action; an answer: it weighs as the argument it answers); the move says how its alternative is better: "comparison": "surely", "sooner" or "cheaper"
  The answer that another action open to the agent would realize the goal more effectively, more surely, sooner or at lower cost (D075, D089); an action merely as good answers nothing (D006). A move made with it records which way the other action is better.
  parts: P = Agent who would take the action (agent, e.g. "the city council"); G = Goal both actions serve (goal, e.g. "lower emissions"); A2 = Other action that would do better (action, e.g. "subsidize plant-based food"); A = Action argued for (action, e.g. "tax meat")
  reads: One of the goals of {P} is {G}; It is possible for {P} to bring about {A2}; Doing {A2} brings about {G}; For {P}, {A2} would realize {G} more effectively than {A}, more surely, sooner or at lower cost; therefore There is a way for {P} to realize the goal {G} more effectively than {A}
  sources: recommended: a source showing the other action would do better
  typical wording: better way, more effective, more effectively, cheaper, sooner, instead, rather than, a better option

AS:bridge_possible_good — From a Possible Good Consequence to the Action (bridge) (action, weight 0.65, as AS:consequences_modal)
  A possible good consequence counts for doing the action when its chance matters enough to the decision (D008). The move does not presume the possibility; an argument from possible positive consequences, a move of its own, supports it.
  parts: A = Action (action, e.g. "introduce a four-day week"); G = Good consequence that may follow (event, e.g. "higher productivity")
  reads: {A} may be worth doing for the sake of {G}; The chance that doing {A} brings about {G} is large enough, given what {G} would be, to bear on whether {A} should be done; therefore {A} should be done
  unless (exceptions the other side may argue): It is worth finding out first whether action {A} would bring about {G}, and until then that possibility should not count in deciding on the action: it can be found out in time, reliably enough to settle the question, at a cost and risk worth bearing
  typical wording: worth the chance, worth a try, might pay off, could pay off

AS:bridge_possible_harm — From a Possible Bad Consequence to Not Acting (bridge) (action, weight 0.65, as AS:negative_consequences_modal)
  A possible bad consequence counts against doing the action when its chance matters enough to the decision (D008). The move does not presume the possibility; an argument from possible negative consequences, a move of its own, supports it.
  parts: A = Action (action, e.g. "license the pesticide"); G = Bad consequence that may follow (event, e.g. "harm to bees")
  reads: {A} may be unwise to do because of {G}; The chance that doing {A} brings about {G} is large enough, given what {G} would be, to bear on whether {A} should be done; therefore {A} should not be done
  unless (exceptions the other side may argue): It is worth finding out first whether action {A} would bring about {G}, and until then that possibility should not count in deciding on the action: it can be found out in time, reliably enough to settle the question, at a cost and risk worth bearing
  typical wording: not worth the risk, too risky, better safe than sorry, the risk is too great

AS:consequences — Argument from Positive Consequences (action, weight 0.65)
  An action should be performed because it brings about good consequences.
  parts: A = Action (action, e.g. "introduce a carbon tax"); G = Good consequence (event, e.g. "cleaner air")
  reads: Doing {A} brings about {G}; {G} is good; therefore {A} should be done
  unless (exceptions the other side may argue): The action {A} has bad consequences that outweigh {G}; In deciding on action {A}, {G} is too slight a consequence to count; In deciding on action {A}, the gain {G} counts for less because of whom it would go to
  sources: recommended: a source showing the action brings about the consequence
  typical wording: consequence, consequences, would lead to, will lead to, leads to, result in, results in, benefit, benefits, good outcome, because it would

AS:consequences_modal — Argument from Possible Positive Consequences (action, weight 0.65, as AS:consequences)
  An action may be worth doing because it may bring about a good consequence. Its conclusion bears on the decision only through the bridge from a possible good, which carries it there when the chance matters enough (D008).
  parts: A = Action (action, e.g. "introduce a four-day week"); G = Good consequence that may follow (event, e.g. "higher productivity")
  reads: Doing {A} may bring about {G}; {G} is good; therefore {A} may be worth doing for the sake of {G}
  unless (exceptions the other side may argue): The action {A} has bad consequences that outweigh {G}; In deciding on action {A}, {G} is too slight a consequence to count; In deciding on action {A}, the gain {G} counts for less because of whom it would go to
  sources: recommended: a source showing the action could bring about the consequence
  typical wording: may lead to, might lead to, could lead to, may bring, might bring, could bring, possibly, a chance of, potential benefit

AS:expert_opinion — Argument from Expert Opinion (truth, weight 0.70), can back an answer to any question
  A claim is plausible because an expert in its field asserts it.
  parts: W = Expert or credible source (entity, e.g. "the IPCC"); D = Field of expertise (domain, e.g. "climate science"); S = Proposition asserted (proposition, e.g. "human activity is warming the planet"), filled in for you when the argument answers a question or is about a statement
  reads: {W} is an expert in {D}; {S} is a matter of {D}; {W} says that {S}; therefore {S}
  also assumed: {W} says that {S}, and this is based on evidence
  unless (exceptions the other side may argue): {W} is not a trustworthy source; Other experts disagree that {S}
  sources: recommended: where the expert asserts it (a citation or a link)
  typical wording: expert, experts, scientist, scientists, according to, study, studies, research, professor, doctor, dr, researchers, ipcc, peer reviewed

AS:finding_out_first — Argument for Finding Out First (action; an answer: it weighs as the argument it answers)
  The answer that a possible consequence should be found out before it counts in the decision, since an investigation would settle it in time, reliably enough and at a cost worth bearing (D095 (3), on the owner's declaration under D053). It defeats both bridges about the same action and consequence. A bare claim that the consequence could be found out is not this scheme, and the game refuses it at the question.
  parts: I = Investigation that would settle it (entity, e.g. "a six-month trial in one office"); A = Action decided on (action, e.g. "switch to a four-day week"); G = Possible consequence to find out about (event, e.g. "higher productivity")
  reads: {I} would settle, reliably enough for the decision, whether doing {A} brings about {G}; {I} can be done before the decision on {A} must be taken; The costs and risks of {I} are worth bearing to know whether doing {A} brings about {G} before that possibility counts in the decision; therefore It is worth finding out first whether doing {A} would bring about {G}, and until then that possibility should not count in deciding on {A}
  sources: recommended: a source on the investigation, its timing and its cost
  typical wording: find out first, wait and see, a trial, a pilot, test it first, study it first

AS:good_outweighs_bad — Weighing a Good Consequence against a Bad One (value; an answer: it weighs as the argument it answers)
  The answer that a good consequence of the action matters more than the harm it is argued against for (C003, D064, D075). It concludes the exception good_outweighs(A,G) of the argument it answers.
  parts: A = Action (action, e.g. "introduce a carbon tax"); H = Good consequence that matters more (event, e.g. "cleaner air"); G = The consequence it outweighs (event, e.g. "higher heating bills")
  reads: Doing {A} brings about {H}; {H} is good; {H} matters more than {G}; therefore Doing {A} has good consequences that outweigh {G}
  sources: recommended: a source showing the action brings about the good consequence
  typical wording: outweigh, outweighs, matters more, worth it anyway, the gain is greater

AS:negative_consequences — Argument from Negative Consequences (action, weight 0.65)
  An action should not be performed because it brings about bad consequences (the counterpart of positive consequences).
  parts: A = Action (action, e.g. "introduce a carbon tax"); G = Bad consequence (event, e.g. "higher heating bills for poor households")
  reads: Doing {A} brings about {G}; {G} is bad; therefore {A} should not be done
  unless (exceptions the other side may argue): The action {A} has good consequences that outweigh {G}; In deciding on action {A}, {G} is too slight a consequence to count; In deciding on action {A}, the harm {G} counts for less because of whom it would fall on
  sources: recommended: a source showing the action brings about the consequence
  typical wording: bad consequence, bad consequences, would cause, would harm, harm, harmful, danger, dangerous, risk, backfire, should not, shouldn't, downside

AS:negative_consequences_modal — Argument from Possible Negative Consequences (action, weight 0.65, as AS:negative_consequences)
  An action may be unwise to do because it may bring about a bad consequence. Its conclusion bears on the decision only through the bridge from a possible harm, which carries it there when the chance matters enough (D008).
  parts: A = Action (action, e.g. "license the pesticide"); G = Bad consequence that may follow (event, e.g. "harm to bees")
  reads: Doing {A} may bring about {G}; {G} is bad; therefore {A} may be unwise to do because of {G}
  unless (exceptions the other side may argue): The action {A} has good consequences that outweigh {G}; In deciding on action {A}, {G} is too slight a consequence to count; In deciding on action {A}, the harm {G} counts for less because of whom it would fall on
  sources: recommended: a source showing the action could bring about the consequence
  typical wording: may cause, might cause, could cause, may harm, might harm, could harm, risk of, a chance of, potential harm

AS:other — Other (your own scheme) (truth, weight 0.50), can back an answer to any question
  An argument that fits none of the listed schemes: write its premises and conclusion yourself. It is recorded for finding new schemes.
  parts: P1 = Premise 1, in your own words (proposition); P2 = Premise 2, in your own words (optional) (proposition); P3 = Premise 3, in your own words (optional) (proposition); P4 = Premise 4, in your own words (optional) (proposition); P5 = Premise 5, in your own words (optional) (proposition); P6 = Premise 6, in your own words (optional) (proposition); C = The conclusion, in your own words (proposition), filled in for you when the argument answers a question or is about a statement
  reads: {P1}; {P2}; {P3}; {P4}; {P5}; {P6}; therefore {C}

AS:position_to_know — Argument from Position to Know (truth, weight 0.65), can back an answer to any question
  A claim is plausible because someone in a position to know asserts it.
  parts: W = Knowledgeable source (entity, e.g. "a local resident"); D = Domain of knowledge (domain, e.g. "what happens in the village"); S = Proposition asserted (proposition, e.g. "the road floods every spring"), filled in for you when the argument answers a question or is about a statement
  reads: {W} is in a position to know about {D}; {W} says that {S}; {S} is a matter of {D}; therefore {S}
  unless (exceptions the other side may argue): {W} is dishonest
  sources: recommended: where they assert it (a citation or a link)
  typical wording: witness, saw, eyewitness, insider, told me, reported, was there, first hand, firsthand, knows, in a position to know, official

AS:practical_reasoning — Practical Reasoning (action, weight 0.70)
  An agent should do an action because, in the current circumstances, it brings about a state that realizes one of the agent's goals, which promotes a value.
  parts: P = Agent who would take the action (agent, e.g. "the city council"); G = Goal to be realized (goal, e.g. "a stable climate"); S1 = Current circumstances (state, e.g. "emissions are rising"); A = Action to be performed (action, e.g. "introduce a carbon tax"); S2 = Future state after action (state, e.g. "lower emissions"); V = Value promoted by the goal (value, e.g. "public health")
  reads: One of the goals of {P} is {G}; The current situation is {S1}; Doing {A} in the situation {S1} would lead to {S2}; The goal {G} would be achieved in {S2}; Achieving {G} would promote the value {V}; therefore {A} should be done
  also assumed: {V} is a legitimate value; {G} is a worthy goal; It is possible for {P} to bring about {A}
  unless (exceptions the other side may argue): There is a way for {P} to reach the state {S2} more effectively than {A}; There is a way for {P} to realize the goal {G} more effectively than {A}; There is a way for {P} to promote the value {V} more effectively than {A}; The action {A} has bad consequences that outweigh {G}; Another goal of {P} is incompatible with {G}
  typical wording: should, ought to, we must, in order to, so that, goal, aim, achieve, promote, policy, plan to

AS:practical_reasoning_goal — Instrumental Practical Reasoning (action, weight 0.65)
  An agent should do an action because, in the current circumstances, it brings about a state in which the agent's goal is realized (goal-based, without values: Walton 2015; the book's practical inference, 22.1). For an argument that also names the value the goal promotes, use Practical Reasoning.
  parts: P = Agent who would take the action (agent, e.g. "the city council"); G = Goal to be realized (goal, e.g. "meet the 2030 climate target"); S1 = Current circumstances (state, e.g. "emissions are rising"); A = Action to be performed (action, e.g. "introduce a carbon tax"); S2 = Future state after the action (state, e.g. "lower emissions")
  reads: One of the goals of {P} is {G}; The current situation is {S1}; Doing {A} in the situation {S1} would lead to {S2}; The goal {G} would be achieved in {S2}; therefore {A} should be done
  also assumed: It is possible for {P} to bring about {A}; {G} is possible
  unless (exceptions the other side may argue): There is a way for {P} to reach the state {S2} more effectively than {A}; There is a way for {P} to realize the goal {G} more effectively than {A}; Something else would have to happen, or be done, before {A} could achieve {G}; The action {A} has bad consequences that outweigh {G}; Another goal of {P} is incompatible with {G}
  sources: recommended: a source showing the action would bring about the state
  typical wording: in order to, so that, so as to, means to, the way to, to achieve, to reach, our goal, the aim

AS:sign — Argument from Sign (causality, weight 0.60)
  Something is probably true because an observed sign usually indicates it.
  parts: A = Observable sign or indicator (event, e.g. "wet streets"); B = Indicated condition (event, e.g. "it rained"), filled in for you when the argument answers a question or is about a statement
  reads: {A} is observed; {B} is generally indicated when {A} holds; therefore {B} holds in the current situation
  also assumed: {A} and {B} are strongly correlated
  sources: recommended: where the sign was observed
  typical wording: sign, signs, indicates, indication, suggests, symptom, evidence of, shows that, points to, observed

AS:values — Argument from Values (value, weight 0.60)
  A value that the agent judges positive is a reason to keep a goal it favours.
  parts: V = Value being invoked (value, e.g. "fairness"); A = Agent or judger (entity, e.g. "most voters"); G = Goal affected (goal, e.g. "equal pay")
  reads: {V} is a positive value for {A}; {V} supports the goal {G} for {A}; therefore {V} is a reason to keep the goal {G}
  typical wording: value, values, freedom, fairness, justice, equality, dignity, important to, matters, principle, right thing

## Your reply
Think it through, then end your reply with one JSON object. An example; use the arguments, questions and references of this game:
{
  "context": ["what you observe on the board that matters for this move", "…"],
  "thoughts": ["your reasoning, step by step", "…"],
  "summary": "one or two sentences: the situation, your reasoning and your move",
  "expect": [{"stmt": "s1", "label": "out"}],
  "alternatives": [{"action": {"type": "question", "target_arg_id": "a1", "answers_cq_id": "CQ:premise_acceptable", "target_premise_id": "s2"}, "why_not": "…"}],
  "confidence": 0.6,
  "action": {"type": "attack", "target_stmt_id": "s2", "scheme_id": "AS:position_to_know", "variable_bindings": {"W": "…", "D": "…"}, "text": "your argument in a sentence or two, as the other player will read it", "evidence": ["a source, if any"]}
}
- "action" is your move; it is the only required field. "type": "support" (a new argument; with a target and a question, a defence; with target_stmt_id, an argument for the statement), "attack", "question", "abstain" (pass) or "resign".
- Leave out of variable_bindings the answer part and the parts a statement fixes: the game fills them in.
- Statements can be given by reference ("s3", "¬s3") or by ID. "text" is your argument in your own words; "evidence" lists your sources. Both are shown to the other player.
- "expect": the labels you predict for some statements ("claim" for the claim) after your move; they are checked. "alternatives": moves you considered and why you did not make them. "confidence": how likely, from 0 to 1, the move helps your side. These three are optional; they are recorded with the move, to study and improve the game.
- A bare move object, as in protocol 1, is still accepted.

## How the game works
- Every argument is an instance of an argumentation scheme (Walton): you fill in the scheme's parts with short phrases, and the scheme's sentences (listed under "The schemes") are built from them. Its premises hold until someone challenges or attacks them.
- Each scheme has critical questions. To ATTACK an argument, answer one of its questions against it; to DEFEND one, answer a question in its favour. Either way you back the answer with an argument of a scheme the question allows; the answer itself is filled in for you.
- You may ASK a question about a premise or the inference without answering it, or CHALLENGE a premise ("why should we accept that?"): the argument stops counting until its author answers, with any argument for the premise.
- You may argue FOR or AGAINST any statement on the board, as for the claim, with a scheme whose conclusion can be that statement.
- Or put forward a NEW argument, PASS or RESIGN.
- After every move the Carneades engine labels each statement IN, OUT or UNDECIDED. An argument is in force when all its premises are IN and no exception or undercutter against it is IN. A statement that is at issue (argued for and against) is decided by the strongest argument in force on each side, not by their sum: under PE (preponderance) the stronger side wins and a tie leaves both OUT; under CCE it must also lead by more than 0.5; under BRD, also the other side must weigh under 0.3.

- Scores are live: they count what stands now, so points for an argument go when it falls.

The agent who decides is decider (the one who decides whether to take the actions argued about). # WAG: the Waltonian Argumentation Game. It is your move. (wag-protocol/2)

You are Pro. You argue FOR the claim: you win if the claim is IN when the game ends. Mode: debate. Round 2 of 4. Scores: Pro 0.0; Con 2.0;

## How the game works
- Every argument is an instance of an argumentation scheme (Walton): you fill in the scheme's parts with short phrases, and the scheme's sentences (listed under "The schemes") are built from them. Its premises hold until someone challenges or attacks them.
- Each scheme has critical questions. To ATTACK an argument, answer one of its questions against it; to DEFEND one, answer a question in its favour. Either way you back the answer with an argument of a scheme the question allows; the answer itself is filled in for you.
- You may ASK a question about a premise or the inference without answering it, or CHALLENGE a premise ("why should we accept that?"): the argument stops counting until its author answers, with any argument for the premise.
- You may argue FOR or AGAINST any statement on the board, as for the claim, with a scheme whose conclusion can be that statement.
- Or put forward a NEW argument, PASS or RESIGN.
- After every move the Carneades engine labels each statement IN, OUT or UNDECIDED. An argument is in force when all its premises are IN and no exception or undercutter against it is IN. A statement that is at issue (argued for and against) is decided by the strongest argument in force on each side, not by their sum: under PE (preponderance) the stronger side wins and a tie leaves both OUT; under CCE it must also lead by more than 0.5; under BRD, also the other side must weigh under 0.3.
- Make your parts true and relevant to the discussion, in plain words: the other player can challenge any of them. Cite sources when a scheme asks for them.
- The debate is about the claim: pro wins if it is IN when the game ends, con otherwise; the scores do not decide it. The game ends after round 4, when a side resigns, or when a side passes while the verdict is against it.
- Scores are live: they count what stands now, so points for an argument go when it falls.

## Who decides
The agent who decides is decider (the one who decides whether to take the actions argued about). A recommendation ("A should be done") is addressed to the agent, so the actions you argue about are the agent's; the game fills in the agent's place (P) itself. The alternatives are compared in this situation: the present one.

- You may ASK a question about a premise or the inference without answering it, or CHALLENGE a premise ("why should we accept that?"): the argument stops counting until its author answers, with any argument for the premise.
- You may argue FOR or AGAINST any statement on the board, as for the claim, with a scheme whose conclusion can be that statement.
- Or put forward a NEW argument, PASS or RESIGN.
- After every move the Carneades engine labels each statement IN, OUT or UNDECIDED. An argument is in force when all its premises are IN and no exception or undercutter against it is IN. A statement that is at issue (argued for and against) is decided by the strongest argument in force on each side, not by their sum: under PE (preponderance) the stronger side wins and a tie leaves both OUT; under CCE it must also lead by more than 0.5; under BRD, also the other side must weigh under 0.3.
- Make your parts true and relevant to the discussion, in plain words: the other player can challenge any of them. Cite sources when a scheme asks for them.
- The debate is about the claim: pro wins if it is IN when the game ends, con otherwise; the scores do not decide it. The game ends after round 4, when a side resigns, or when a side passes while the verdict is against it.
- Scores are live: they count what stands now, so points for an argument go when it falls.
